subject: VPC egress & proxy certificate questions for private endpoint integration
messages:
From: Paul Singh <paul.singh@greenline.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>
Cc: Zoe Park <zoe.park@netsecure.io>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Questions on VPC egress model + cert pinning for private endpoint integration

Marissa / David,

Thanks for the walkthrough yesterday — Greenline is starting to scope out the onboarding for a private runtime and we have a few specific asks from our SecOps team around outbound controls. I put the high-level requirements into the attached workbook (greenline-eval-egress-requirements.xlsx) but wanted to call out the ambiguous bits so we can decide on a pattern: 

1) Static egress IPs vs. proxy: can Redwood provide a narrow set of static IPs for control-plane callbacks (we'd prefer IP allowlisting in our firewall), or do you recommend customers terminate through an outbound proxy (we have an existing proxy fleet)?

2) mTLS / client certs: SecOps asks whether mutual TLS is supported for private control-plane connections (i.e., will the runtime present a client cert to redwood control endpoints), and how certificate rotation is handled.

3) SNI and TLS inspection: Our perimeter team performs TLS inspection for some hosts — will the SNI on the outbound connection be stable and suitable for SNI-based inspection rules, or does Redwood recommend TLS passthrough to prevent interception?

4) DNS vs. IP allowlist: if we rely on FQDN-based egress (control.redwood.ai), our environment does split-horizon DNS. Which approach reduces operational burden for both sides?

If you can reply with a recommended pattern and any example firewall rules, that would be great. If it's easier, we're available for a 30-minute sync this week.

Paul Singh
Head of Platform Security, Greenline Systems
paul.singh@greenline.com
+1 (415) 555-0198

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Paul Singh <paul.singh@greenline.com>, David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 11:03:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Questions on VPC egress model + cert pinning for private endpoint integration

Paul — thanks, good set of questions. I attached our current egress IP block list (redwood-egress-ip-blocks.csv) and a short acceptance checklist to make the next steps explicit. TL;DR: we support both models but recommend a two-phased approach for lower operational friction.

Recommended pattern (phases):

- Phase 1: Proxy / mTLS gateway (fast, fewer firewall changes). Configure your perimeter proxy to allow outbound TCP:443 to our control plane FQDN (control.redwood.ai) and terminate the outgoing TLS to our gateway. We support mTLS from runtime -> proxy -> control: the runtime can be configured to present a client cert when connecting to the control plane if you run a proxy that supports client cert forwarding. This avoids immediate IP-level changes on your side.

- Phase 2: Allowlist egress IPs for hardened posture. Once you’re comfortable, transition to explicit IP allowlisting to reduce reliance on a middlebox. We publish a small set of egress CIDR blocks that we keep stable for private deployments; updates are announced with a 48–72 hour window.

Notes about your specific asks:
- Static egress IPs: yes, for private deployments we can reserve a /24 block per customer as part of Dedicated/Private packages. If you don't have Dedicated, we can provide a narrower rolling pool with announced change windows.
- mTLS & rotation: we support client certs at the control plane. Rotation is handled by the runtime agent: we provide a cert-rotation API and can coordinate automated rotation with your Ops team. The runtime will accept a PKCS#12 bundle or work through your proxy if you prefer.
- SNI & TLS inspection: we typically recommend TLS passthrough to preserve end-to-end authenticity for model payloads; however, SNI from the runtime is stable (control.redwood.ai). If your TLS interceptor rewrites SNI, that can break mTLS pinning, so plan to exempt control.redwood.ai from any active MITM.
- DNS vs IP allowlist: FQDN-based is easier initially, but IP allowlisting is more robust for compliance audits. If you run split-horizon DNS, share the resolution behavior and we can validate the FQDN resolves to our published ranges.

Next steps I propose:
1) You share the completed greenline workbook and your proxy auth method.
2) David will produce example firewall rules and a short iptables sample you can test.
3) Schedule a 30-minute technical check-in to validate NAT/DNS behavior.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
Director, Solutions Engineering — Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai
Attachment: redwood-egress-ip-blocks.csv; egress-acceptance-checklist.md

From: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.ai>
To: Paul Singh <paul.singh@greenline.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:45:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Questions on VPC egress model + cert pinning for private endpoint integration

Paul / team — below are concrete examples that should help your firewall team. These assume you adopt Phase 2 (explicit allowlist) eventually; Phase 1 works with the same FQDN but you’ll route through your proxy.

Example outbound rules (minimal):
- Allow TCP 443 from runtime subnets (10.10.0.0/16) -> Redwood egress CIDR 34.212.180.0/24 (control plane endpoints)
- Allow outbound DNS (UDP 53) to your resolver only (we recommend no public DNS egress to internet resolvers)
- If using proxy: allow runtime -> proxy on 3128 (or your proxy port) and proxy -> control.redwood.ai:443

Sample iptables snippet (attachment: sample-iptables.sh):
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -s 10.10.0.0/16 -d 34.212.180.0/24 --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp -s 10.10.0.0/16 --dport 53 -j ACCEPT

Notes on NAT and DNS:
- If your runtime is behind NAT, the outbound source IP observed by Redwood will be the NAT egress IP. For strict IP allowlisting, ensure the NAT egress is static (elastic IP) and share that with us; we can pin to that for per-customer routing.
- FQDN resolution: control.redwood.ai resolves to our egress pool. If split-horizon DNS resolves to internal addresses in your VPC, confirm whether your resolver will return public egress addresses for outbound connections that leave the VPC — we can validate via a short curl test from a bastion.

mTLS specifics:
- Our control plane accepts client cert authentication via TLS client certs (X.509). The runtime can perform a handshake with a client cert if configured. For proxy deployments where the proxy terminates TLS, you can configure the proxy to re-establish mTLS to Redwood and either forward a client cert or use a short-lived token issued by Redwood during bootstrap.
- Certificate rotation: we recommend automating rotation using our cert-rotation API. The rotation window can be customized; for FedRAMP-like postures we do 30-day rotation by default.

Operational checklist for onboarding (summary):
1) Confirm NAT egress IP(s) and share them with Redwood.
2) Confirm whether TLS interception will be performed; if yes, request an exemption for control.redwood.ai or plan proxy-based mTLS.
3) Validate DNS resolution from a bastion and share results.
4) Run a smoke test: curl -vk https://control.redwood.ai/health from your bastion and capture SNI + cert chain.

Happy to walk the firewall team through this — recommend a 30 min call with your SecOps + infra.

-David Kim
Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference
david.kim@redwood.ai
Attachment: sample-iptables.sh

- David will own the iptables sample and a short verification script (he's attached sample-iptables.sh).
- Marissa will coordinate the kickoff and track the acceptance checklist in the Drive doc.

Can we tentatively book a 30-minute call Monday 11/16 at 10:00 PT for a run-through with your SecOps and our infra? If that works, I'll send a calendar invite and include a short runbook for the smoke test.
